body:
Aug 21, 2026 3:26am PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									Getty Images
	

		
	
				
	Meghan Markle is eyeing a return to the screen as she and Prince Harry move back to the U.K., Variety has confirmed.

	Following the shock announcement on Wednesday that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are returning to England after six years in California, Australian outlet News.com.au reported on Friday morning that Meghan has been “offered a role in an upcoming project based in the U.K.” Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied this report, though further details are being kept under wraps for now.
	

	Meghan is best known for her breakout role as Rachel Zane in the legal drama “Suits,” which she starred in for seven seasons from 2011 to 2018. After marrying Prince Harry in 2018, she largely stepped back from acting, though she’s set to make a cameo as herself in the upcoming Amazon MGM comedy “Close Personal Friends” with Brie Larson and Lily Collins. Recently, she’s also hosted the Netflix lifestyle series “With Love, Meghan,” which launched her brand As Ever, and appeared as a guest judge on “MasterChef Australia.” 


	Harry and Meghan are expected back on U.K. soil in the coming weeks, with their young children Archie and Lilibet enrolled in school beginning in September. The move is said to be for an “extended period,” though the couple will retain their home in Montecito, California, and don’t intend to relocate their production banner Archewell or As Ever to the U.K. They will remain non-working royals after stepping down from official duties in 2020 before their move to the U.S.


	
		More from Variety

title: Canada’s H264 Nabs Colombia’s ‘Where the River Begins’ Ahead of Toronto Fest World Premiere
description: Canadian distributor h264 has pounced on worldwide sales rights to “Where the River Begins” (“Donde comienza el rio”) by Colombian-Canadian filmmake
body:
Canadian distributor h264 has pounced on worldwide sales rights to “Where the River Begins” (“Donde comienza el rio”) by Colombian-Canadian filmmaker Juan Andrés Arango (“La Playa DC”), ahead of its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival (TIFF).

	Starring Girleza Duave Cerezo, Juan David Junca Linares and Ana Michell Nama Dumaza, “Where the River Begins” screens at TIFF’s Centrepiece section, a coveted platform for international cinematic voices.
	

	It follows Yajaira (played by Duave Cerezo), a young Embera woman, who lives with her daughter Maria  (Nama Dumaza) in a rough Bogotá neighborhood. Haunted by dreams of the jungle, Yajaira pines for the village she left behind. After tragedy forces them to flee, she and her daughter embark on a perilous journey to the Andágueda River, accompanied by Jhon (Junca Linares), a charismatic young gang member with a dark secret. The teaser unfolds below:




	Said h264 president Jean-Christophe Lamontagne: “’Where the River Begins” is a bold and deeply rooted film with the ability to resonate far beyond its place of origin. Juan Andrés Arango’s singular vision, combined with the strength of the project, makes us incredibly excited about the film’s international journey as we head into TIFF.”

	“’Where the River Begins’ is a film about the universal search for a place we can call home, told from the singular perspective of a young Embera mother. For me, having this film selected for TIFF represents an ideal starting point for its international journey, at a festival renowned precisely for its great diversity of voices,” Arango told Variety.
	

	“Working with h264 has been a new and stimulating experience as a filmmaker, as I had never before established such a close creative collaboration with a sales agent. Jean-Christophe J. Lamontagne and Léa-Marie Montreuil have been involved since post-production, providing creative input during the final stages of the edit. This has made me feel that h264 is not simply a business partner but an integral part of the film’s team,” said Arango whose career-launching debut feature “La Playa DC” (Cannes 2012, Lions Film Award Rotterdam) represented Colombia at the Oscars. His second film, “X500,” premiered at the 2016 TIFF and scored several wins at a number of festivals.

	Shot in Bogotá, Medellín and Honda among other locations in Colombia by DP Nicolas Canniccioni, the Canadian-Colombian co-production, in collaboration with Norway, was produced by Annick Blanc (Midi La Nuit) and Maria Gracia Turgeon (Midi La Nuit and 12PM) and Paola Andrea Pérez Nieto of Colombia’s Inercia Películas, a producer of Cannes 2015 Caméra d’Or winner “Land & Shade.”

	The 51st Toronto Film Festival takes place over Sept. 10-20.

title: ‘Supporting Role’ Director Ana Urushadze Preps ‘Fear of Butterflies,’ a Detective Story With ‘Mysticism and a Touch of Body Horror’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Georgian director Ana Urushadze (“Scary Mother”), whose Rotterdam prizewinner “Supporting Role” plays in competition this week at the Sarajevo Film
body:
Georgian director Ana Urushadze (“Scary Mother”), whose Rotterdam prizewinner “Supporting Role” plays in competition this week at the Sarajevo Film Festival, is prepping her third feature film.

	“Fear of Butterflies” follows a young woman on the cusp of 30 who is “going through some bizarre things, mentally and physically,” Urushadze told Variety. The director described the film, which explores the mordant consequences of a woman “not accepting her body,” as a “detective story with a little bit of mysticism and a touch of body horror.”
	

	The title riffs on Urushadze’s own “severe fear” of the winged insects, which she has harbored from an early age. Recently, she explained, she tried to tackle her phobia with the help of a psychologist friend, who posited the question: If a butterfly was a human being, what would it be like?


	“I was like, ‘What kind of question is this?’” the director said, laughing. “But then, weirdly, I knew the answer. I told him a butterfly would be a very sick person, an invalid. Either very ill or handicapped. And he said, ‘That’s it. It’s your fear to be like that.’”

	It was an ah-ha moment for the director, an avowed hypochondriac. “Something clicked,” she said — although that hasn’t helped to conquer her phobia.

	“Fear of Butterflies” will reunite Urushadze with Estonian producer Ivo Felt’s Tallinn-based shingle Allfilm, a co-producer on “Supporting Role.” With a bitter rift dividing the Georgian film industry, which has witnessed a long-running boycott by many directors, producers, actors and other industry professionals against the state-backed Georgian National Film Center, the director said she’s looking abroad for financing — and isn’t even certain if the film will be made in Georgia. “I’m really open to anything,” she said.
	

	It is a bittersweet prospect for Urushadze, whose much-feted feature debut “Scary Mother,” which won the prize for best first feature at Locarno in 2017 as well as the top honors in Sarajevo, was described by Variety’s Jessica Kiang as “a startling debut that wholly earns its place as standard-bearer for one of the most exciting and distinctive national cinemas to have emerged in recent years.”

	For her follow-up, “Supporting Role,” a Tbilisi-set nocturne starring a captivating Dato Bakhtadze, Urushadze follows “a lumbering movie star on a surreal and wryly melancholic soul-search,” as described by Variety’s Beatrice Loayza, praising the “mesmerizing effect” of the director’s moody, meandering drama in a glowing review. It arrives in the main competition in Sarajevo after winning a Special Jury award and the FIPRESCI prize at Rotterdam in January.

	“Supporting Role” shares more than just mordant comedy and a growing haul of festival accolades with its predecessor, which tells the story of a middle-aged woman who finds freedom in the act of writing her first novel. It was during the auditions for “Scary Mother” that Urushadze conducted a search for an elderly man to play the role of the protagonist’s father. The search turned sour when one of the actors was put off to discover a young, inexperienced woman sitting in the director’s chair. 

	The man turned down the role, but gifted Urushadze with an encounter whose “weird tension of young meets old” would provide the spark for “Supporting Role.” The film follows Niaz (Bakhtadze), a once-famous star of Georgian cinema who embarks on a bizarre and fatalistic odyssey of self-transformation, after an unsettling audition with a young female director looking to cast him in a minor part. 

	Though topical in its exploration of a very contemporary theme — that of a man of faded glories discovering the world has passed him by — “Supporting Role” is above all a riveting character study. Urushadze presents a sympathetic portrait of Niaz, a man who once embodied a certain type of swaggering masculinity but now seems adrift in the modern world. 

	Inhabiting the role with “tremendous gravitas,” in the words of Loayza, Bakhtadze almost seems born for the part. Yet it was a stroke of luck that brought the actor into Urushadze’s orbit.
	

	“I had three other actors in mind — amazing actors. But things didn’t work out,” the director said. “In the end, there was like one month and a half left [until shooting began], and we didn’t have an actor. It was crazy. Then Dato appeared out of the blue.”

	The chemistry between the two was apparent. “It clicked immediately,” Urushadze said, acknowledging now that she “can’t imagine anyone else” playing the part of Niaz. 

	And despite the film’s premise — and the title’s promise — it didn’t hurt that Bakhtadze still boasts the charisma and screen presence of a leading man. “The camera loves him.”

	The Sarajevo Film Festival runs Aug. 14 – 21.

schema.headline: ‘Supporting Role’ Director Ana Urushadze Preps ‘Fear of Butterflies,’ a Detective Story With ‘Mysticism and a Touch of Body Horror’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Kenneth Branagh on Doing His Own Stunts as a KGB Operative in ‘Mayday,’ Bonding With Ryan Reynolds Over Soccer: ‘We Can Be Pretty Nerdish’
description: While he may not be known as an action star, Kenneth Branagh absolutely wanted to give it a go for “Mayday,” his upcoming Apple TV Cold War action-c
body:
While he may not be known as an action star, Kenneth Branagh absolutely wanted to give it a go for “Mayday,” his upcoming Apple TV Cold War action-comedy in which he co-stars with Ryan Reynolds. He just needed to find out how best to get involved.

	“I asked the directors, ‘What’s the way to do it if you’re a man of a certain age and it’s not your natural genre?'” Branagh said, speaking at the Variety Lounge at Edinburgh International Film Festival. Their answer: “Get here early.”
	

	So he did, to, as he explained, “start making the body a bit more flexible,” adding that he wanted to at least give the impression that his character was a “former lethal KGB operative” and “possible assassin, when necessary.” Branagh said it ended up being “very, very interesting and fun to be involved in the advanced choreography,” and that getting there early did indeed make a difference. “The stunt guy said: ‘We’ve never had an actor for this long.’ I said, ‘I’m that scared.'”

	“Mayday,” being released by Apple TV on Sept. 4, is set in the Soviet Union in 1987 and follows Reynolds’ crashed U.S. Air Force Pilot as he teams with Branagh’s former ex-KGB man — someone he describes as a “‘Top Gun’-loving exile in the forest of Siberia” — to escape.

	While not throwing themselves around the snow in Canada, where the film mostly shot, Branagh and Reynolds bonded over a love of soccer, with Branagh being an avid lifetime supporter of Tottenham Hotspur and Reynolds as co-owner of Wrexham alongside Rob McElhenney.

	“That was a source of, for me, fascination, at how they were living the dream,” said Branagh, who recalls the very first press conference when the new Wrexham co-owners said that they hoped to take the club from non-division football to the Premier League. “The snorts of derision were involuntary and fun, but now here they are in the Championship [the second tier below the Premier League]. Come on, this is quite something. So yes, we can be pretty nerdish about the beautiful game.”
	

	Branagh was in Edinburgh as the recipient of the festival’s inaugural outstanding contribution to cinema award, but also for the 30th anniversary screening of his 1996 adaptation of “Hamlet,” being shown in its full, unbridged four-hour version (with an interval).

	“Hamlet” famously starred a 20-year-old, pre-fame Kate Winslet, who Branagh said he’d auditioned for his 1994 film, “Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein,” but at just 17 she was too young. “She, perhaps uniquely, is the person who walked into the room and brought with them a sense of self possession, not arrogance, but just sort of being fully present,” he said. “She seemed to have a maturity beyond her years.”

	It was while working on “Hamlet,” on a day that Winslet was shooting a “mad scene,” that the career-changing call came through from James Cameron to say she would star alongside Leonardo DiCaprio in “Titanic.” It’s a moment Branagh said he remembers vividly.

	“There was a lot of talk about this enormous film that was going to happen, and we were all big fans of Cameron’s. And you felt, we’re at a little pivotal moment,” he said. “There was a smell about ‘Titanic’ that — aside from its name, its director and the subject — it would be very special. The casting search had already been something that had become a sort of legend in its own terms.”

	Branagh recalled taking Winslet aside following the “Titanic” call and saying: “Enjoy every moment up until the premiere of that movie, because your life will change after it.”

	As he added to Variety: “I hope it wasn’t a depressing thing to hear!”

schema.headline: Kenneth Branagh on Doing His Own Stunts as a KGB Operative in ‘Mayday,’ Bonding With Ryan Reynolds Over Soccer: ‘We Can Be Pretty Nerdish’

title: Folk Horror ‘Wolf Days,’ Family Drama ‘The First Week of August’ Win at Sarajevo Industry Awards
description: Emilija Gašić’s folk horror “Wolf Days” and Filip Mojzeš’ family drama “The First Week of August” won the top prizes in the Sarajevo Film Festival’s
body:
Emilija Gašić’s folk horror “Wolf Days” and Filip Mojzeš’ family drama “The First Week of August” won the top prizes in the Sarajevo Film Festival’s CineLink Industry Days, the industry section focused on projects in different stages of development from Southeast Europe, the Middle East and North Africa.

	Gašić’s sophomore feature, which is produced by Serbia’s Non-Aligned Films and co-produced by Istok Films and Restart, won the Eurimages Co-Production Development Award, a cash prize of €20,000 ($23,000).
	

	The film follows a woman facing menopause who turns to a folk healer who draws her into a series of increasingly ridiculous rituals, driving her to the edge of madness in search of her own liberation. Gašić’s first feature, “78 Days,” premiered in the Bright Futures section of the Intl. Film Festival Rotterdam. 


	In a director’s statement provided to Variety, Gašić said: “‘Wolf Days’ is inspired by my encounters with many women who have been misdiagnosed, dismissed and misunderstood within a deeply patriarchal healthcare system. This film seeks to uncover and challenge the taboos surrounding women’s health, especially menopause, and to expose the power imbalances that define both medical and personal relationships.”

	The Eurimages Special Co-Production Development Award, also a cash prize of €20,000 ($23,000), went to “Mamayi,” from Ukrainian writer-director Oleksandr Roshchyn and producer Packgauz. Set in 2009, the film follows two TV reporters forced into a dirty election campaign for a pro-Russian candidate who struggle to stay honest with their work and the people. 
	

	The film marks the directorial debut of Roshchyn, known as the cinematographer behind films including 2021 Berlin Crystal Bear winner “Stop-Zemlia” and 2025 Berlin Golden Bear contender “Timestamp.”

	“During a lengthy assignment in Ukraine, I began observing and imagining the personal drama of a journalist unfolding against the backdrop of pivotal socio-political events,” Roschchyn said in a director’s statement. “[‘Mamayi’] is a film about witnessing the approach of a catastrophe — about the ability to foresee it and the inability to prevent it.”

	In the Works in Progress strand, the HBO Award in the amount of €30,000 ($35,000) went to Filip Mojzeš’s “The First Week of August” (pictured), produced by Tamara Babun Zovko and Matija Drniković for Wolfgang&Dolly and Black Photon. The family drama is set during an idyllic island vacation that takes a tumultuous turn when a mother’s sudden physical outburst towards her 10-year-old son exposes hidden tensions and lingering conflicts within the family.

	As with his previous short films, which premiered in competition at Sarajevo, Mojzeš’ feature debut “also explores complex family dynamics,” he said in a director’s statement. “In that sense, the film represents a natural continuation of my ongoing preoccupation with the fragility of the nuclear family.”

	Also in Works in Progress, the Post Republic Award, offering €30,000 ($35,000) in post-production services, went to “The White Week,” directed by  Bojan Vuletić and produced by  Jelena Mitrović, Boris T. Matić, Lana Matić, Danijel Hočevar and Ivan Đurović for Film House Baš Čelik, Propeler Film, Vertigo and Artikulacija. The film follows an 11-year-old boy who exploits his brother’s tragic death to fight his father and his community, until his lies expose the hypocrisy and corruption beneath a seemingly moral society.

	The Avanpost Media Award, offering €30,000 ($35,000) in post-production services, went to Kazakh director Assel Aushakimova’s “Pay the Bill,” produced by Assel Yerzhanova for Film Film Film. It tells the story of a 65-year-old woman who receives an unexpected late-night phone call from a police officer, leading to a difficult night and day searching for her daughter that plunges her into a world of general indifference.
	

	Other prizes handed out in the CineLink Co-Production Market include the Film Center Montenegro Award, which gave a €10,000 ($11,700) cash prize to Turkish director Selcen Ergun’s “How to Disappear in the Lake.” The Kosovo Cinematography Center CineLink Award in the amount of €10,000 ($11,700) went to “The Taste of the Peach,” by Georgian filmmaker Elena Mikaberidze, who also received the Next Step Studio CineLink Award. The Artekino International Prize in the amount of €6,000 ($7,000) went to “Forbidden Fruit,” from Slovenia’s Urška Djukić Lecamus.

	In the CineLink Drama strand, the Croatian Audiovisual Center Drama Award in the amount of €15,000 ($17,500) went to the family drama series “You Can Always Come Back,” from creator Tena Gojić and writer Hana Jušić. The TV Drama Vision Pitch Award went to the Croatian political thriller “Stringers,” from writer-creator Nikola Kuprešanin.

	Lastly, the Female Voices CineLink Award, a €20,000 ($23,000) cash prize handed out in partnership with the Slovenian Film Center and the United Nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, went to the horror-comedy series “Little Yugoslavia,” from writer-creators Teona Strugar Mitevska and Sonja Prosenc.

	The Sarajevo Film Festival runs Aug. 14 – 21.

schema.headline: Folk Horror ‘Wolf Days,’ Family Drama ‘The First Week of August’ Win at Sarajevo Industry Awards

title: Sriram Raghavan Developing New Thriller in the ‘Johnny Gaddaar’ Zone for India’s Matchbox Shots as ‘Operation Safed Sagar’ Soars on Netflix Charts (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indian auteur Sriram Raghavan is developing a new thriller for Matchbox Shots set in the tonal zone of his 2007 film “Johnny Gaddaar,” as the Mumbai
body:
Indian auteur Sriram Raghavan is developing a new thriller for Matchbox Shots set in the tonal zone of his 2007 film “Johnny Gaddaar,” as the Mumbai production house grows its slate on the strength of the global Netflix success of war series “Operation Safed Sagar.”

	“Johnny Gaddaar” was a twist-laden neo-noir heist thriller that marked Neil Nitin Mukesh’s screen debut alongside Dharmendra, and has since grown into a cult favorite. 


	“I am personally working on a couple of subjects with them,” Raghavan tells Variety. “One is a true crime sort of thing which I am sort of adapting in my own way. And the other is a fiction, it is a thriller, and I mean next year is 20 years of ‘Johnny Gaddaar,’ so something I want to do in that zone.” The director has yet to settle on a title.
	

	Beyond the Raghavan projects, Matchbox’s slate includes a second season of “Scoop” for Netflix with Hansal Mehta, a still-untitled dark comedy thriller from Vasan Bala and another untitled thriller directed by Jasmeet Reen. 

	Matchbox’s Sanjay Routray says the range is deliberate. “We want to cater to a diverse audience, both in India and internationally,” he says. “The common thread across all those titles is that each one is an untold or uniquely told story with genuine entertainment value. The genre changes, the scale changes, the format changes. The promise to the audience does not.”

	Meanwhile, Raghavan traces his relationship with Matchbox back to its earliest days when it was known as Matchbox Pictures. “Matchbox began, I mean as a company, with ‘Andhadhun,'” he says. “So we tasted success very, very early, and I am very happy that now ‘Safed Sagar’ is like doing sort of similar sort of wave, creating waves in the OTT [streaming] kind of a thing.”
	

	The 2018 blind-pianist thriller “Andhadhun” became the company’s breakout hit, grossing $62.4 million worldwide, against a production budget of INR160 million ($1.7 million), a return the company has since held up as the benchmark for the rest of its slate. Much of that total came from an unexpected market: released in China in 2019 under the title “Piano Player,” “Andhadhun” opened to $10.6 million and went on to gross $47.1 million there, more than three times its India total of $13 million, at the time making it the fifth-highest-grossing Indian film ever released in the Middle Kingdom, trailing only “Dangal,” “Secret Superstar,” “Bajrangi Bhaijaan” and “Hindi Medium.”

	Routray points to “Andhadhun” as his go-to example of finding commercial potential in unlikely material. “On paper, a thriller about a blind pianist sounds like a niche festival film,” he says. “On screen, ‘Andhadhun’ became a global blockbuster. The hook was always there. It was just about believing in the director and backing the story with everything we had.”

	Raghavan also directed the Matchbox-produced “Merry Christmas,” with Routray producing, and was involved with “Monica, O My Darling.” “It is a comfort zone for me,” Raghavan says. “I work there, Sanjay is a friend of mine, and we know each other for many, many years.”

	Netflix series “Operation Safed Sagar” was filmed inside active air force installations under strict operational protocols, using actual MiG fighter jets alongside cockpit simulation technology built specifically for the production. Routray says the shoot, which involved a crew of more than 450 people working at altitudes above 16,000 feet, tested the limits of what the company had built over the years. “At that height there is no existing infrastructure,” he says. “Logistics, power, accommodation, safety, medical support, all of it had to be created from scratch and then sustained for a long-haul shoot. It also proved to us, and to our partners, that Matchbox can deliver at that scale.”

	By its second week on the platform, the series had climbed to No. 2 on Netflix’s global chart for non-English shows, landed in the top 10 in 40 territories and stayed at No. 1 in India. It’s the second consecutive Matchbox series to reach those heights: Anubhav Sinha’s “IC 814: The Kandahar Hijack” also debuted at global No. 2 and India No. 1, a feat Matchbox says makes it the only Indian production house to place back-to-back series near the top of Netflix’s worldwide charts.
	

	The company’s push beyond Hindi-language projects produced its first Malayalam-language film, “Thrishanku,” a romantic comedy starring Arjun Ashokan and Anna Ben that Matchbox produced alongside Lacuna Pictures and Clock Tower Pictures & Co. Written and directed by Achyuth Vinayak, the film released in theaters in 2023, following a couple whose plan to elope is complicated when the man’s sister decides to elope as well. Matchbox has also been acquiring book rights, including “The Gurugram School Murder” and “The Johnson and Johnson Files,” as it builds out a pipeline of owned intellectual property, the same approach that turned the book “Flight into Fear” into “IC 814.”

	For Matchbox’s Patil, success today comes down to one word. “Longevity,” she says. “Stories that stay with audiences long after the release window has passed. In our experience, if a story achieves longevity, the numbers and the recognition tend to follow on their own. They are outcomes, not targets.”

	That philosophy extends to how the company spends. Patil says Matchbox invests in development on projects long before a greenlight or outside funding arrives, money committed with no guarantee of a return. “We know exactly how much we can afford to lose on a bet, and we never bet more than that,” she says. “That is what allows us to keep taking punts year after year.” Routray adds that the discipline cuts both ways: “For any film to land, there has to be a perfect marriage between the numbers and the creative intent. If either side of that equation is broken, we would rather walk away early than force a project into existence. Some of our best decisions have been the films we did not make.”

	Routray also points to a fact he thinks audiences rarely register: overall theatrical footfalls have declined even as the cost of going to the cinema has risen. “The film has to be worth leaving the house for,” he says. “That reality shapes what we greenlight and how we make it, far more than people realize.”

	Matchbox is also exploring animation, AI-assisted production and other emerging formats, while recommitting to theatrical releases alongside its streaming slate. Summing up the company’s next five years, Routray keeps it to three words: “Content remains constant.”

schema.headline: Sriram Raghavan Developing New Thriller in the ‘Johnny Gaddaar’ Zone for India’s Matchbox Shots as ‘Operation Safed Sagar’ Soars on Netflix Charts (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Woody Harrelson Ready to Direct Another Live Film, Compares Jason Bateman’s ‘The Cackling of the Dodos’ to Martin McDonagh and the Coen Brothers
description: Almost a decade after taking on an unusually challenging directorial debut with the world’s first live-streamed feature film in “Lost in London,” Wo
body:
Almost a decade after taking on an unusually challenging directorial debut with the world’s first live-streamed feature film in “Lost in London,” Woody Harrelson is finally ready to direct again. The actor revealed his desire to be back behind a camera, as well as his latest creative venture as a budding stand-up comic, while at the Variety Lounge, presented by the Sarajevo Film Festival and BH Telecom. 

	Despite having a career spanning more than 100 films, starring in major franchises such as “The Hunger Games” and “Star Wars,” leading TV hits such as “True Detective” and “Cheers,” and now hosting a podcast, Harrelson said directing “Lost in London” was “the most challenging thing I have ever experienced.” 
	

	To celebrate the 10th anniversary of his debut, Harrelson is thinking about revisiting the format, albeit in a less dramatic fashion. “I’ll go to one of the streamers and say: Hey, do you want to try doing a live film? Maybe like an hour, though, and certainly not like [‘Lost in London’], when there were 14 different locations and hundreds of extras.”

	“It nearly killed me,” he recalled of directing and starring in the high-pressure shoot. “I think it could be fun to try it again, but this time I think it will be easier having the benefit of having done it before and knowing 190 things I would have done differently. I can hopefully fix it, make it better.”

	On the subject of stressful new ventures, Harrelson has recently taken on a new practice: stand-up comedy. “I have a lot of friends who do stand up and I admire them a lot,” he said. “To me, it’s the most difficult, challenging form of entertainment because it’s you, a microphone, and the audience. And you’ve got to make them laugh. Anyway, I’ve been making notes and everything. I am sure I’m going to just absolutely crash the first time, but I think I’ll try.”
	

	Can we expect a one-hour comedy special anytime soon? “I haven’t even tried it!,” he exclaims. “No! Can’t expect the special [laughs].”

	We can expect some comedy, however, with Harrelson set to appear on Apple TV’s latest comedy series “Brothers.” The series reunites Harrelson with “True Detective” co-star Matthew McConaughey to play fictionalized versions of themselves. In the show, created by “The Office” producer Lee Eisenberg, their friendship is put to the test once they uncover a decades-old secret: they might actually be brothers.

	The story is inspired by real-life events, coming to the screen a few years after Harrelson went public with the fact that his father met McConaughey’s mother just around the time the “Dallas Buyers Club” actor was conceived. Harrelson had known McConaughey’s mother for 25 years when she pulled him to one side and told him she knew his dad. “I’m thinking, well, that’s weird that she’s never told me this. I’m thinking, well, what’s behind this story?” 

	Has working with McConaughey in a series loosely inspired by their own lives meant learning something new about each other? “I don’t know if we learned anything new,” he said. “I mean, we’ve been hanging out a long time, and we’re very good friends. I guess I learned that he’s one of the funnest people I know. I love hanging out with him. I can barely get enough of him. And he is very much like my brother. I think the show turned out real good.”

	Another Harrelson project to look forward to is Jason Bateman’s “The Cackling of the Dodos,” which marks another big reunion: with Sam Rockwell, with whom he shared the screen in “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.”

	The Netflix film is the first production under Harrelson’s new banner, Children at Play, which he launched with “Champions” producer Anna Schwartz. The producer found the script, which Harrelson said was “pretty good.” He told Schwartz he would do the film if she got Rockwell to sign on, which she did. Then, Harrelson asked for Bateman to direct. And Schwartz booked the “Ozark” star. 

	Harrelson was particularly elated to get Bateman, whom he called “the guy with the Midas touch.” “They did a rewrite, and it really became fantastic. Much more like a Martin McDonagh or Coen Brothers type of vibe. I think that one’s going to be real good. I have a good feeling about it.”

schema.headline: Woody Harrelson Ready to Direct Another Live Film, Compares Jason Bateman’s ‘The Cackling of the Dodos’ to Martin McDonagh and the Coen Brothers

title: Jacob Elordi Ducks James Bond Question at London World Premiere of Ridley Scott’s ‘The Dog Stars’ When Asked if He’s Been Auditioning: ‘I’m Here on Holiday’
description: Jacob Elordi was the star guest in London on Thursday night as he touched down for the world premiere of Ridley Scott‘s latest feature “The Dog Star
body:
Jacob Elordi was the star guest in London on Thursday night as he touched down for the world premiere of Ridley Scott‘s latest feature “The Dog Stars.”

	The actor’s arrival in Leicester Square was immediately soundtracked by the noise of screams from fans, including from a group of girls leaning out of nearby window, who dramatically upped both their volume and pitch when the actor turned to wave at them. The actor also sparked swoons when he walked and posed on the carpet with Rak Jasper, one of three acting dogs who appear in the movie. 
	

	Alongside Elordi, “The Dog Stars'” other cast — including Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley and Guy Pearce — were in attendance at the Odeon Luxe cinema, together with the legendary director himself (who premiered his last movie, “Gladiator 2,” in the same spot less than two years ago).


	Speaking to Variety, Elordi described Scott as “the king of movies,” saying that working with him was “such a treat — a dream come true.”

	He added: “I don’t think I’ll ever have an experience like that. Yeah. He’s one of a kind and he’s a pioneer of of modern cinema.”

	With the casting for James Bond now very much underway and Elordi continuing to have a strong presence among the favorites for the coveted role, Variety also managed to sneak in a question about whether he’d been involved in the auditions. It was a query he, clearly with some experience now under his belt, expertly ducked. “I’m here on holiday,” he said with a smile. 



	

					Photo by Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for The Walt Disney Company Limited
									Getty Images for The Walt Disney
	



	“The Dog Stars,” from Disney’s 20th Century Studios, is a post-apocalyptic sci-fi, directed by Scott from a screenplay by Mark L. Smith and based on Peter Heller’s 2012 novel of the same name. The film is set in the aftermath of a devastating flu pandemic that has almost eradicated humanity, and follows a former civilian pilot and hardened ex Marine as they confront outside threats and hold onto the possibility of a better life.
	

	Ironically, Scott had originally eyed his “Gladiator 2” leading man Paul Mescal for the main role, but he had to drop out due to scheduling conflicts with the Beatles’ biopics, and Elordi stepped in.

	Speaking to Empire Magazine before the premiere, Brolin said that he almost quit “The Dog Stars” after just one day due to Scott’s intense filmmaking process. “It bugged me out, and I got really scared,” he said, adding that he called his agent to say “I want out. Something’s really wrong and I’ve got to get the f— out of here.”

	However, he said things settled eventually down enough for him to continue, describing Scott’s approach as “stratospherically creative and stratospherically dangerous.”

	“The Dog Stars” will release in theaters on Aug. 28.

schema.headline: Jacob Elordi Ducks James Bond Question at London World Premiere of Ridley Scott’s ‘The Dog Stars’ When Asked if He’s Been Auditioning: ‘I’m Here on Holiday’

title: ‘The Marching Band’ Review: Brothers From Opposite Worlds Are United by Music in a Finely Tuned French Crowdpleaser
description:
Aug 21, 2026 12:55am PT	
	

	
		‘The Marching Band’ Review: Brothers From Opposite Worlds Are United by Music in a Finely Tuned Fren
body:
Aug 21, 2026 12:55am PT	
	

	
		‘The Marching Band’ Review: Brothers From Opposite Worlds Are United by Music in a Finely Tuned French Crowdpleaser
	

	Belatedly opening Stateside after proving a domestic hit in 2024, Emmanuel Courcol's film succumbs to formula, but is lifted by its precise construction and strong lead performances.
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy of Playtime
	

		
	
				
	“The Marching Band” blasts through more story in its first 12 minutes than many films now manage in two hours. In those first 720 seconds we meet Thibaut (Benjamin Lavernhe), a well-heeled classical music conductor in Paris, who discovers that he will need to find a blood marrow transplant as he has leukemia; he learns that his sister is not a match, as he was adopted; he then discovers a biological brother, Jimmy (Pierre Lottin), who was not adopted and still lives in a disadvantaged working-class community in the north of France; he asks his new-found brother to help him, and Jimmy accepts.That concision is evident in an almost brutally economical edit and in sharp, precise writing which provides narrative elements and deftly sketches character before moving busily on. Just as a marching band keeps time with its feet, so “The Marching Band” strides on, hitting the requisite notes and paying attention to the melody, sure, but especially making sure to hold the beat and keep the show on the road. This attention to rhythm helps director Emmanuel Courcol‘s film to stay true as it navigates some rather rocky terrain, for it is at once a mismatched buddy movie, a socially conscious crowdpleaser in the vein of, say, “The Full Monty,” and a sophisticated psychological drama à la française. 
	

	That the film mostly pulls this off is testament to its formal precision and to a central pairing of actors, in Lavernhe and Lottin, who manage to find subtlety where broad strokes would seem to be called for. More than two years after its Cannes premiere, “The Marching Band” opens theatrically in the U.S. this week through Greenwich Entertainment.Once the film has dispatched its initial premise — the leukemia storyline is essentially a MacGuffin, and soon disappears for a sizable stretch — it can get down to the business of developing a bond between the characters, and establishing its (gentle) social critique. Jimmy, who works as a cook in a canteen, has a musical gift, which throws into sharp relief the different chances both men have been given in life. A scene in which this terse, withdrawn young man is revealed to have perfect pitch is typical of “The Marching Band’s” best qualities in its appealing first hour or so: Thibaut asks his brother to identify the sounds of a honking car or a barking dog, and Jimmy shyly names the correct chords. That pertness should be unbearable, but the scene is written in a minor key and performed by both actors to match, favouring eye contact and murmurs; the sheer brevity prevents it from becoming gloopy or crass.The casting of Lavernhe and Lottin is particularly inspired, as the two performers bring an affect to these characters that mimics the story’s dynamic. Lavernhe, credited as “Benjamin Lavernhe de la Comédie-Française,” comes from a background in classical theatre, and performs his role with worldly elegance; Lottin, meanwhile, is a veteran of the popular comedy franchise “Les Tuche”, centering on a working-class family from the north of France. These sensibilities come together in the film’s tight dialogue, as when the two men meet and Thibaut introduces himself: “My name is Thibaut Desormeaux, and two weeks ago I learned I have leukemia…” Jimmy: “Ah, shit.” Thibaut: “Yes.” 


	Lottin is particularly intelligent in articulating Jimmy’s shame at his lack of means and achievement, inflected with pride and a lightly worn resentment that comes out in bursts of passive-aggressive joshing; meanwhile, Lavernhe deftly portrays the well-meaning and likable Thibaut as, conversely, insufficiently ashamed of his good fortune, at least early on: This smooth Parisian bobo does not even perceive how he flaunts his wealth and education.
	

	In parallel, “The Marching Band” depicts a working-class community struggling with poverty and unemployment, for whom the musical collective — in which Jimmy plays the trombone, alongside his on-off girlfriend Sabrina (Sarah Suco) — has become a lifeline. Thibaut becomes involved, but will he be able to save the band from ruin? Here, the film closely mirrors the 1996 British comedy “Brassed Off,” making it a dead cert that we’ll eventually get a barn-burning finale showing the federating power of music in adversity. 

	Revealing how that comes about would enter spoiler territory, but saying that it happens at all is germane, as it shows that the film finally falls victim to formula. In these pre-ordained moments — a surfeit of montages, an artificial falling-out between the brothers, the occasional dip into the saccharine — “The Marching Band” becomes a touch pleased with itself. The formula works (and the film has the domestic box-office receipts to prove it), but it detracts somewhat from the project’s smarts elsewhere.In a well-presented technical package, plaudits should go to editor Guerric Catala for a cut that attempts to shun sentiment, and to Christel Birot for costumes that smartly outline both character and class differences via the means of double denim or a freshly pressed felted overshirt. The music department, as well as Courcol’s lively directing and writing, must be commended for scenes of the brass ensemble playing and rehearsing, in a constantly dynamic interaction with dialogue. The zippy soundtrack, much like the film itself, veers between surprisingly choice cuts (the aching “I Remember Clifford” by Lee Morgan) and rabble-rousing crowdpleasers (Dalida, or the overture from “Aida”). Ravel’s “Bolero,” which repeats the same phrase over and over again but with tonal differences each time, also features.

title: ‘The Voice of Hind Rajab’ Director Calls Israeli Investigation Into Killing of Palestinian Girl a ‘Smokescreen’: ‘What Is Needed Is Justice’
description: Kaouther Ben Hania, the director of last year’s Oscar-nominated docudrama “The Voice of Hind Rajab” — about the killing of a 5-year-old Palestinian
body:
Kaouther Ben Hania, the director of last year’s Oscar-nominated docudrama “The Voice of Hind Rajab” — about the killing of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl in Gaza by Israeli forces — has rejected the news that Israel is launching an investigation into Rajab’s death, describing it as “a smokescreen.”

	On Wednesday, the Israeli military admitted that its troops had opened fire on the car carrying Rajab and six members of her family in January 2024. Rajab later died following a three-hour call with the Palestinian Red Cross in which she pleaded for help. An ambulance sent to rescue her was also attacked by the Israeli military, killing two medics.
	

	The Israeli Defense Forces repeatedly claimed that its troops had not been in the area at the time of the killings. But investigations by media outlets found evidence that nearby Israeli tanks were responsible, with the death of Rajab becoming one of the most high-profile incidents in the early months of the war in Gaza, prompting outrage around the world.


	“Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by military police criminal investigation division,” the Israeli military said on Wednesday, more than two years after the killing.

	In a statement on her Instagram page, Ben Hania — who used the recording of Rajab’s call to the Red Cross in her film, which would go on to win numerous honors including the grand jury prize in Venice and nominations from both the BAFTAs and Oscars — pushed back against the investigation.
	

	“This announcement is a smokescreen. For more than two years, the evidence has been there: independent investigations, satellite imagery, ballistic analysis. And there was the most devastating evidence of all: Hind’s own voice, describing the Israeli tanks circling around her. What more did we need?” she wrote. “Did we really have to wait for the accused to decide to investigate itself (yes, itself!) before these facts could finally be taken seriously?”

	Ben Hania added: “Meanwhile, the Israeli military continues to kill Palestinians in Gaza, while the occupation intensifies in the West Bank. What is needed now is not a public relations operation. What is needed is justice (delivered by an independent authority) for Hind and for all the victims of the genocide in Gaza.”

schema.headline: ‘The Voice of Hind Rajab’ Director Calls Israeli Investigation Into Killing of Palestinian Girl a ‘Smokescreen’: ‘What Is Needed Is Justice’

title: Natalie Harp's Intimate Letters to President Trump Revealed
description:
Natalie Harp's Letters To Trump
                          'You Are All That Matters To Me' ...
body:
Natalie Harp's Letters To Trump
                          'You Are All That Matters To Me' ...
                          'I Don’t Want To Ever Let You Down'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 21, 2026
                            2:41 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 21, 2026
                                5:27 AM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Natalie Harp penned intimate letters to President Trump ... and now we're seeing them for the first time, and they show Harp's total devotion to Trump, telling him he's all that matters to her and she never wants to let him down. 
      
    
            Trump's executive assistant wrote the 2 alleged letters to the president during or after his May 2023 golf outing at his courses in Scotland and Ireland. The Daily Beast published the letters in full Thursday night.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In one letter, Harp apologizes to Trump, believing she may have upset him during their overseas trip. She wrote that she thought she was the only person left behind at the airport the night before, so she panicked and called Trump while alone in a van at Customs without her passport. She said she should have just contacted the Secret Service.
      

            Harp also wrote she was sorry for stepping onto the golf course instead of riding in a cart. She pleaded with Trump to "please forgive me" if she had done anything else to cause him trouble.
      
    
            She went on to write that she wants "things to always be right between us" and that she's "been distracted all week" while forgetting to eat and sleep at times.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In addition, Harp wrote that she feared Trump had a lower opinion of her after other people made remarks about her, noting that she only wants to bring joy to Trump. She then ended the letter by referring to Trump as “my Guardian and Protector in this life.”
      
    
            In the second letter, Harp thanked Trump for getting her to “unplug” while they enjoyed their time together on the golf course. She wrote, “We could be out on the Course, with no machines, and even forget what time it was! I didn’t have to be "Human Printer," referring to her nickname in the White House because she quickly prints out favorable Trump articles and hands them to the president.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Harp also wrote she could see that Trump noticed her occasional “slightly negative” mood because she's rapidly approaching burnout. She wrote that she envied anyone whose job "seems to be to talk with [Trump] and look pretty," insisting, "I want that job!!”
      
    
            She also wrote that she feels like an "in-betweener" caught between Trump's staff and people who enjoy talking to him on the plane or at dinner. She said the experience harkens back to her days as a talk show host for the ultra-conservative "One America News Network," a job she says she hated.
      
    
            Harp wrapped up the second letter by telling Trump that he has the "absolute right to cuss me out, if need be, when I deserve it, because no one knows or cares about me more.”

schema.headline: Natalie Harp's Intimate Letters to President Trump Revealed

title: Hayden Panettiere: Overdose Crisis Hitting Hard in Neighborhood Where She Died

Hayden Panettiere Death
                          Opioid Crisis Alarms Greenville Locals
body:
Hayden Panettiere Death
                          Opioid Crisis Alarms Greenville Locals
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 21, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hayden Panettiere's death is causing concern for Greenville, SC residents, who fear the actress is just the latest tragic example of the opioid crisis ravaging their city.
      
    
            An addict-turned-advocate who lives in the area tells TMZ ... laced drugs and fatal overdoses have been a serious concern in Greenville for years, particularly in the area where Hayden died last Sunday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She says the area's developed a reputation as a place where people can party and easily obtain drugs ... alleging some residents even have drugs delivered to their doorstep.
      

            While there's currently no hard evidence linking Hayden's death to drugs, a first responder said she suffered a possible overdose, and as TMZ first reported ... the Drug Enforcement Administration is now on the case.
      
    
            The local resident says the city is trying to make medications like Narcan -- which combats opioid overdoses -- more widely available in the community, while also teaching people how to administer it. Fatal ODs actually declined in Greenville last year, and the coroner credits that, in part, to Narcan.
      
    
            In a sad coincidence, August is Overdose Awareness Month, and we're told some Greenville residents plan to commemorate Hayden on August 28 at an annual event called Jessica’s Walk.
      
    
            Officially, the coroner has said Hayden's cause of death is pending toxicology results.

title: Hayden Panettiere's Boyfriend Brian Hickerson Speaks Out After Her Death
description:
Hayden Panettiere
                          Boyfriend Brian Breaks Silence on Her Death
body:
Hayden Panettiere
                          Boyfriend Brian Breaks Silence on Her Death
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 20, 2026
                
                            11:41 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 21, 2026
                                5:13 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Brian Hickerson is breaking his silence following the death of Hayden Panettiere ... but he isn't saying much.
      
    
            Brian's attorney, Sloan Ellis from the Ellis Hinton law firm, tells TMZ ... "Hayden's death remains under investigation and it is important to allow that investigation to proceed."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The statement continues ... "As has been publicly reported, police confirmed there were no signs of foul play."
      
    
            It ends ... "Out of respect for Hayden's loved ones and the ongoing investigation, there will be no further comment at this time."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Ellis is a former federal prosecutor who has worked hand-in-hand with the DEA and FBI on past cases ... which is notable, considering we first reported that the DEA has joined the multi-agency investigation.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            As we first told you ... Brian and his brother, Zach Hickerson, were both at the South Carolina apartment when Hayden died. Brian was asleep in the other room and Zach came in to find her unresponsive on an armchair.
      
    
            First responders tried to save her, but she was ultimately pronounced dead at the scene ... and Brian reportedly became visibly emotional as efforts to save her came to an end.
      
    
            Police say Brian showed them a bag of medications Hayden was taking before she died.
      
    
            Brian and Hayden had a long, complicated history together.
      
    
            The two began dating in 2018, and their relationship later became the subject of multiple domestic violence cases involving Brian.
      
    
            Brian isn't saying all that much here ... as investigators continue trying to piece together what happened leading up to Hayden's death.
